Day 110 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

A Word's Job in the Sentence

藉搭配與句中功能辨別抽象字義。

This week's review cards are preserve, beneath, validity, donor, and restore. The class has used them in quotations, experiments, visitor notices, and exhibit records. Their teacher now asks students to match the words with fresh sentences rather than copying the examples they already remember.

One sentence describes keeping a speaker's intended meaning in a shorter quote. Preserve fits. Another places a measuring device under a cloth square, making beneath the right choice. The students explain that the first word names an action, while the second shows a position.

A card about how long a pass remains usable needs validity. A person giving an object to a collection is a donor. To put a missing name back from a trusted record is to restore it. Students identify the clues before checking the cards.

The final challenge removes one clue from each sentence. Pairs discuss whether the answer is still clear and which added detail would help. They discover that knowing how a word works in a sentence can support reading even when its topic is unfamiliar.

Day 111 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Science Fair Title Debate

使標題強度符合實際研究證據。

The science fair team has tested three paper bridges made with different folds. Their best bridge holds eighteen small blocks in the classroom test. Nori wants the display title to read The Strongest Bridge in the World because she thinks visitors will notice it immediately.

Her teammate argues that the title promises more than their work shows. They have compared only three designs, all made from the same paper and tested with the same blocks. They have not tested every paper bridge, much less every real bridge.

The group proposes A Fold That Helped Our Paper Bridge Hold More. It sounds less dramatic, but it invites a question the team can answer with its measurements. They add photos of all three designs and explain what happened when each bridge finally bent.

At the fair, a visitor asks whether thicker paper would change the ranking. The students say that would require another test. Their honest answer leads to a useful discussion, and Nori realizes that a careful claim can make a project more interesting rather than less.

The Refill Pack Comparison

區分總價與單位價格，將需求納入購買。

At a stationery shop, Mei compares two refill packs for her pen. A small pack contains four refills and costs sixty dollars. A large pack contains ten and costs one hundred and thirty. Both contain the same type of refill, and each refill fits her pen.

The large pack has a lower price per refill, but Mei needs only three before the school year ends. She will change to a different pen next year, so extra refills may not be useful. Her budget for today's purchase is one hundred dollars.

A friend offers to share the large pack and take six refills while Mei keeps four. They agree to divide its price according to the number each receives. The shop will sell the sealed pack to them together; they can separate the refills after paying.

Mei calculates her share before agreeing. Buying more is not automatically a saving, but a planned split can change the comparison. She checks that her friend really wants the same refill type and writes their agreement down.

Renewed, but Not Forever

Library chat: I clicked Renew on my borrowed book this morning. Does that mean I can keep it for another two weeks? The website showed a spinning circle, and I closed the page before any result appeared. My original due date is tomorrow.

Day 114 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Letter Behind the Lens

區分看見的影像與物件本身的變化。

In a classroom demonstration, Bao places a printed letter on the desk and looks at it through a handheld magnifier. At one position, the letter appears larger. He sketches what he sees, then moves the lens slightly and notices that the view changes.

The teacher asks whether the printed letter itself has grown. Bao measures its height with a ruler after setting the lens aside. The ink still occupies the same space on the page. What changed was the view through the lens, not the physical size of the printing.

The class records the lens position for each drawing. Students try to keep the page and their viewing position steady while changing the lens distance. They describe the image before offering an explanation, and they do not use a drawing as a direct measurement of the ink.

Bao adds two labels to his notes: object and observed image. The distinction helps him explain why a larger-looking letter does not require a larger printed page. Careful observation includes recognizing what the tool changes about the way something is seen.

Day 115 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

An Audio Walk You Can Pause

理解自助導覽的路線、安全與使用方式。

NEIGHBORHOOD AUDIO WALK: Download the six recordings before leaving the community center. The route begins at the old fountain and ends at the reading garden. Each recording describes one stopping point. You may pause, repeat, or skip a recording and still follow the printed route map.

The complete route is about two kilometers and usually takes forty minutes without stops. The recordings add eighteen minutes altogether. Your total visit will be longer if you pause to draw, rest, or talk. The route is not a timed race, and no finish time is required.

Listen only while standing at a marked stopping point, not while crossing a street. Keep enough awareness of the surroundings to hear people nearby. If a path is closed, follow the posted detour and use the map; an old recording may still describe the usual route.

The free printed map is available at the front desk until four. Downloading the recordings is also free. The reading garden closes at five, so plan your departure time with any extra stops in mind.

Boss: Two Notices for One Lost Bag

LOST NOTICE: A student left a dark green sports bag near the east gym door after lunch. It has a silver zipper and a white number seven on one side. Inside are a yellow towel and a water bottle. The student asks finders to contact the school office.

FOUND LOG: At one thirty, a volunteer records two bags. Bag A is green with a black zipper and contains a blue towel. Bag B is dark green with a silver zipper, a white seven, and a yellow towel. Both are now held at the office.

Day 117 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

One Detail Is Not the Whole Picture

綜合本週字詞理解核對與判斷。

The review group prepares five cards: renewal, steady, detour, hidden, and handover. Their task is to explain the words through short actions. A reader must be able to understand the situation without seeing the lesson from which the word originally came.

A student waiting for a later library due date is checking a renewal. Someone keeping a page from moving holds it steady. A walker using an alternate path around roadwork follows a detour. The group keeps each explanation focused on the action that matters.

For hidden, they describe a bag detail that has not been made public. Handover belongs beside the moment a checked item is returned to its owner. One student says the act of finding a bag is already a handover, but a partner points out that no receiver is involved yet.

The students add a receiver to the sentence and read it again. They finish by asking what extra detail makes each word fit. This small habit helps them avoid choosing an answer merely because it belongs to the general topic of the passage.

Day 118 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Survey Box Left Blank

區分未回覆、無意見與反對的資料意義。

The student council asks each class whether it wants a lunchtime chess corner. The form offers yes, no, and need more information. At the deadline, twenty classes have replied and four have not. The council secretary puts the missing four under no to make the table complete.

During the meeting, Pia asks whether those classes actually rejected the idea. Nobody has received their answers. Some may have missed the message or not held a discussion yet. An empty box does not tell the council what the class thinks.

The secretary adds a separate not yet received category and sends the four classes a short reminder. The council reports the answers it has, together with the response count. It also lists the questions raised by classes needing more information.

By the next day, three missing classes respond and one still has no answer. The final announcement keeps that distinction visible. The council can decide how to proceed under its rules, but it should not invent an opinion to make a chart look finished.

Day 119 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Used Puzzle Check

用清單驗證二手物品，區分描述與確認。

At a neighborhood secondhand sale, Amos finds a puzzle box labeled complete. The picture has one hundred large pieces, and the seller says her family finished it last winter. Amos wants it for his younger cousin, who enjoys puzzles but becomes frustrated when a piece is missing.

The box has been opened since that winter. Amos asks whether they can count the pieces together before buying. The seller agrees and spreads them across a clean table in groups of ten. They count ninety-nine pieces, then find one more under the folded instruction sheet.

Now they have the stated one hundred pieces, but Amos knows counting alone cannot prove every piece belongs to that picture. The seller offers a photo of the family's completed puzzle and says he may return it the same afternoon if a mismatch is found.

Amos buys it after confirming the return arrangement and the seller's table number. He checks it at home with his cousin. The label was useful, but asking respectful questions gave him a clearer basis for deciding.

Day 120 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

The Interview in Two Languages

區分逐字引述、翻譯與摘要。

Project chat: Our interview was in Chinese, but the presentation must be in English. I translated the resident's answer into one short sentence. May I put quotation marks around it? The answer in the recording is much longer and includes a reason for her opinion.

Teacher: A translation should preserve the meaning, and a summary should be labeled as a summary. Do not present your shortened interpretation as the exact words someone spoke. Keep the original recording and explain how you used it.

Writer: She said the market was convenient for daily shopping but too crowded during holiday evenings. My sentence says she dislikes the market. Teacher: That leaves out the useful part and broadens her complaint beyond a particular time.

Writer: I will write that she values ordinary shopping there but wants less crowding on holiday evenings. I will label it an English summary and check the meaning against the recording. The original language should not disappear from our source notes.

Day 121 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Air, Sunlight, and the Reading

辨認測量對象與感測器環境。

In a classroom scenario, two groups try to compare the air around the same school bench. One places a thermometer in direct sunlight on the wooden seat. The other hangs an identical thermometer under a nearby cover, away from contact with the bench.

After ten minutes, the readings differ. The first group says the air beside its thermometer must be much warmer. The teacher asks what else differs between the setups. Sunlight can affect the instrument, and contact with the seat adds another condition.

The class does not discard either reading. It labels exactly where and how each was taken. If the goal is a more consistent air comparison, the groups need matching placement and protection from direct sunlight, rather than changing several things at once.

Their revised notes separate the target question from the procedure. A number displayed on a tool is not automatically an answer to every question about the surroundings. Students must understand what the setup allows that number to represent.

Boss: What the Club Vote Shows

以投票規則、回覆狀態與假設情境推論。

CLUB RULE: A new weekend activity requires support from more than half of all fifty members. Each member may submit one response. The options are support, oppose, or undecided. Members who do not reply are recorded separately rather than counted as opposing the activity.

FIRST RESULTS: Forty members respond. Eighteen support the proposal, twelve oppose it, and ten are undecided. Ten members have not replied. An early announcement says the proposal has enough support because supporters are the largest group among the three response options.

REVIEW MESSAGE: Being the largest response group is not the same as meeting the rule. The committee asks undecided and missing members for a final answer by Friday. Existing supporters and opponents keep their recorded choices unless they request a correction before the deadline.

For a planning exercise, students consider what would happen if all ten undecided members changed to support while everyone else's response stayed the same. They keep this hypothetical result separate from the actual tally, since the final responses have not arrived yet.

Day 124 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Cards for Careful Claims

區分已知、假設與需確認的資訊。

The review team selects five words: interpretation, consistent, substitution, undecided, and hypothetical. They place the words beside short descriptions from different projects. A student explains that the cards do not all describe facts of the same kind; some describe an action or a state of knowledge.

An English sentence summarizing a longer interview is an interpretation that must remain faithful to the source. Measurements taken with matching methods are more consistent. Replacing one registered swimmer with another is a substitution, not permission to add an extra person without checking.

A member who has replied but has not chosen a side is undecided. A possible vote count imagined for analysis is hypothetical. The group keeps these separate from no response and from the current official count, which describe different situations.

For the last exercise, partners underline every word that tells them whether something has happened, might happen, or needs approval. They compare explanations before seeing answers. Accurate reading sometimes depends on a small status word as much as on the larger topic of a passage.

Day 125 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Coupon That Starts Tomorrow

核對優惠有效期及最低消費條件。

At a school book fair, the visiting bookshop gives Hugo a coupon for twenty dollars off a future purchase of at least two hundred dollars. The coupon starts tomorrow and expires at the end of the month. It cannot be used with another coupon, and it gives no cash change.

Hugo's current books cost one hundred and eighty dollars. He considers adding a thirty-dollar notebook to reach the minimum and use the coupon now. The cashier points to the starting date. Buying an extra item today would not make the coupon valid earlier.

Hugo pays for the books he needs and keeps the coupon separately. The next week, he plans to buy a dictionary priced at two hundred and twenty dollars. Before relying on the discount, he checks that the date falls inside the coupon period and that the dictionary is eligible.

He spends two hundred dollars on the dictionary after the discount. The extra notebook was never needed. Hugo learns that a threshold and a valid date are separate conditions; meeting one does not automatically satisfy the other.

The Bus Stop Name Has Moved

以路線方向與現場標示核對乘車資訊。

A city changes the name of a bus stop near Mara's home from Library Corner to Civic Center. The stop itself remains in the same place. Mara sees the new name on a digital map and assumes the bus now follows a different road.

At the stop, a notice explains that only the name has changed. The route number and travel direction are unchanged. However, the stop across the road serves the opposite direction, so choosing by the shared place name alone can still lead to the wrong bus.

Mara checks the route number, direction arrow, and next two stops before boarding. She tells her grandfather about the new name and marks the familiar library building on a small map. He recognizes the landmark even though the printed stop name is unfamiliar.

Later, Mara updates a meeting message without saying the stop moved. She writes new name, same location and includes the direction toward the station. The short clarification preserves what people already know while pointing out exactly what they need to notice.

Day 128 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Averages on the Class Thermometer

由每日數據理解平均值無法呈現的差異。

Two groups record the classroom temperature at three fixed times in a pretend data exercise. Room A's readings are twenty, twenty-four, and twenty-eight degrees. Room B's are twenty-three, twenty-four, and twenty-five. The groups use the same units and label each reading with its time.

Both rooms have an average reading of twenty-four degrees. Eli says that means the rooms stayed equally comfortable throughout the day. His partner asks whether an average shows how widely the individual readings differ or how each person felt.

They calculate the difference between the highest and lowest readings. Room A's spread is eight degrees; Room B's is two. This does not directly measure comfort, but it shows that identical averages can hide different patterns of change.

For their report, the students show the three original readings beside the average. They also state that comfort was not surveyed. The summary becomes more useful because readers can see what it includes and which questions still need different evidence.

Day 131 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Unchanged Detail Hunt

辨別版本差異、持續有效事項及相對位置詞。

For review, the class chooses five words: interchangeable, spread, revision, allocation, and occupied. The teacher gives pairs an old notice and a new notice. They must list which details changed and which remained valid, instead of assuming that a new heading replaces every earlier instruction.

Revision belongs beside a corrected version of the notice. Allocation describes how tables or stations are assigned. Occupied tells readers that a station is already in use during a particular period. The students draw a short timeline to explain why two bookings conflict.

A separate example uses spread for the difference between the highest and lowest temperature readings. Interchangeable describes things that can replace each other for a purpose. The class notes that two similar photos may not be interchangeable when their approved audiences differ.

Each pair finishes by writing one sentence about an unchanged detail. They underline the evidence for keeping it, just as carefully as the evidence for changing another detail. Accurate updating requires both kinds of attention, especially when several notices refer to the same event.

Day 132 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

Paper for Another Draft

從處理流程推論兼顧節省與隱私的做法。

The class collects paper that is blank on one side for rough drafts. At first, students put every partly used sheet into a shared tray. The pile grows quickly, and everyone celebrates the amount of paper they think they have saved.

When Bess takes a sheet, she notices a classmate's family phone number on the reverse side. Another sheet contains a draft letter with personal information. The teacher pauses the collection and asks the class to sort the sheets before placing them in a public tray.

They keep clean, nonpersonal practice pages for reuse. Sheets containing private details go back to their owners for appropriate disposal. The class adds a clear instruction above the tray and assigns two volunteers to check new additions each afternoon.

The amount of reusable paper is smaller than the original pile, but the system now serves its purpose more carefully. Bess writes that saving resources works best when the process also respects the people whose information may appear on them.

Day 133 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

One Cup, Two Sizes

理解單位定義並換算食譜中的容量。

While making soup with his father, Evan reads an old recipe that asks for three cups of water. He reaches for a large drinking cup and begins to fill it. His father points to a note at the bottom: in this recipe, one cup means two hundred milliliters.

The drinking cup holds two hundred and fifty milliliters when full. Three of those would add more water than the recipe specifies. They find a measuring jug with clear milliliter marks and decide to use the stated volume rather than count ordinary cups.

Evan pours six hundred milliliters into the pot. He then checks the other ingredients, because the word cup might otherwise lead him to repeat the same mistake. The recipe's measurements depend on its defined unit, not on whichever container happens to be nearest.

After lunch, he rewrites the water line as six hundred milliliters, followed by three recipe cups in brackets. The extra explanation will help another family member follow the old instructions without needing to remember the size of a particular drinking cup.

Day 135 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

A Faster Melt with Two Changes

辨認多項條件同時改變造成的歸因問題。

In a classroom scenario, a team compares two equal ice cubes. One sits on a metal tray near a sunny window, while the other sits on a wooden board in a shaded corner. The team measures the time until each cube has completely melted.

The cube by the window melts first. Kai says this proves the metal tray is the only reason. His partner points out that the location changed as well as the surface. The team cannot tell from this comparison how much each difference contributed.

They propose four setups: metal in sunlight, metal in shade, wood in sunlight, and wood in shade. Equal ice cubes would start together, and the team would record all four results. This would help them compare one factor while keeping the other consistent.

The first trial remains in the notebook as an observation with limits. The students explain why the new design answers a clearer question. A result can be real even when the explanation first attached to it is too confident.

Day 136 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Shared Printer Queue

依佇列規則、截止與確認資訊安排工作。

SHARED PRINTER NOTICE: The library printer handles ordinary student jobs in the order received. A job enters the queue only after the desk has checked the file and confirmed the page count. Uploading a file by itself does not reserve a place.

Urgent school notices may be inserted ahead of ordinary jobs by library staff. Students cannot mark a personal project urgent to move it forward. If an urgent notice delays a confirmed job by more than thirty minutes, the desk will send a revised pickup estimate.

The printer accepts jobs of up to thirty printed sides. Longer documents must be divided into separate files and may not finish together. Check that page numbers continue correctly across the files. The desk does not add missing pages from a second version automatically.

At four, the desk stops accepting new jobs, but already confirmed work continues until four thirty. A job still unfinished then is held for the next school day. Please collect only after receiving a ready message, even if an earlier estimate has passed.

Day 138 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Queue Card Review

用語境分辨順序、狀態、臨時安排與影響因素。

The review class works with five words: volume, temporary, factor, queue, and confirmed. A teacher gives them five mini-situations and asks for the clue that makes each choice necessary. Several situations include numbers, but numbers alone do not determine the word.

A measuring jug showing how much water is needed points to volume. A path used only during bridge repairs is temporary. A possible influence on an ice cube's melting time is a factor. The students explain why an influence is different from the observed result itself.

A line of checked print jobs is a queue. A job whose file and page count have been accepted is confirmed, although it may not yet be finished. One student almost writes ready, then notices that the sentence says nothing about completed printing.

For the final check, pairs invent a new sentence that separates confirmed from ready. They read each other's versions and look for evidence of the stage reached. This practice helps prevent a familiar word from quietly adding a fact that the text never states.

The review class works with five words: volume, temporary, factor, queue, and confirmed.

The review class works with five words: volume, temporary, factor, queue, and confirmed.

  4. Printing always finishes before file checking.

Day 139 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Leader Who Listened Last

推論提問順序如何影響團體意見表達。

When the class chooses a project topic, its leader speaks first and explains why she prefers a history display. Several classmates nod, and the next few suggestions sound similar. Jo wonders whether everyone independently favors history or whether the opening speech has narrowed the discussion.

At the next meeting, the teacher asks students to write one idea privately before anyone speaks. The leader then collects the notes without names and reads the range of suggestions. They include a nature map, an interview series, and an experiment display as well as history.

The class discusses the strengths and work required for each idea before voting. The leader speaks after the others this time and explains her preference without presenting it as the group's decision. Students are allowed to change their minds after hearing new reasons.

History still wins, but the path to the decision is clearer. Jo does not claim the first meeting forced anyone to agree. She notices that a different discussion process gave more ideas a visible place before the class made its choice.

Day 140 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Shoes That Fit Yesterday

核對商品尺寸資訊與實際試穿情境。

Before buying indoor shoes for a school performance, Nao checks the size printed inside her everyday shoes. She orders the same number from a different brand and expects a perfect fit. When the pair arrives, her toes feel crowded even though the label matches.

The shop's guide says sizes can differ between styles and asks customers to compare foot length with the specific product chart. It also advises trying the shoes with the socks planned for use. Nao had checked only the number, not the chart or the intended socks.

She keeps the soles clean while trying them indoors and reads the exchange conditions before wearing them outside. The shop accepts unworn returns within seven days with the box and receipt. Her mother helps her measure and select a different size from the actual chart.

Nao exchanges the pair and records the model as well as the size for future reference. She learns that a familiar label is useful information, but it does not replace checking whether a particular item fits the purpose and situation.

Day 141 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

The Source We Haven't Opened

區分搜尋摘要、原始資料與已核實資訊。

Report chat: A search result says the town clock was built in 1890. I have copied that year onto our slide. The result title looks official, but I have not opened the page yet. It might save time if we use the short summary.

Editor: Open the page before relying on it. The year may refer to a renovation rather than the first construction. Check the sentence around the number and identify who published the information. We need a source that actually supports our specific statement.

Writer: The page says the clock was repaired in 1890 and first installed in 1872. The summary left out that distinction. I will change the slide to 1872 for installation and keep 1890 only in the repair timeline.

Editor: Good. Add the source title and link to our notes, then check the other copied dates too. A convenient summary can help locate material, but it should not silently replace reading the evidence behind a claim.

Day 142 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Paper Helicopters on a Timer

由重複量測辨別差距與測量不確定性。

In a classroom scenario, two paper helicopters have different blade lengths. Students drop each from the same marked height onto a clear floor. One student releases the models without pushing, while another uses a hand timer to record how long each takes to land.

The first model's three times are 2.1, 2.2, and 2.1 seconds. The second's are 2.2, 2.1, and 2.2. A student calls the second design definitely better because its average is slightly higher. Her partner asks how precisely a hand timer can distinguish such small differences.

The group repeats the trials and records who times each drop. They also film a few releases for later checking with the teacher. The class does not change the earlier numbers to make the two sets look either more different or more alike.

The report says the observed difference is small and may be affected by timing. More careful measurement is needed before a strong ranking. Learning to recognize uncertainty helps the students decide what to improve in the next test.

Day 145 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

Capacity Is Not a Reservation

複習數據總量、程序狀態與替換。

The reading club reviews five words: source, uncertainty, reservation, capacity, and replacement. Students receive a pretend event file with a room map, a visitor list, and a report quoting a resident. They must decide which document helps explain each word.

The room map shows capacity, the largest number of people its seats can hold. The confirmed visitor list shows reservations, which may total less than capacity. A canceled family's place filled by another accepted family illustrates a replacement, not a new physical table.

For source, students point to the original interview behind the report's quotation. Uncertainty belongs in a note explaining that a travel estimate may change with traffic. One student confuses possible visitors with confirmed visitors and revises the sentence after comparing the list with the map.

The group writes that a number should have both a label and a status. Forty possible seats, twenty-six confirmed people, and two waiting families answer different questions. Careful reading preserves those differences instead of treating every number as a count of the same thing.

Day 146 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

A Larger Page for the Same Story

理解學習工具差異與相同任務目標。

During a reading activity, the teacher gives Nico a larger-print copy of the same story the class is using. His classmates have standard-size pages. One student asks whether the bigger sheet includes easier questions or extra hints, because it looks different from everyone else's worksheet.

The teacher shows that the text and questions are the same. The larger print changes how the material is presented, not what students are asked to understand. Nico can also move his page closer without affecting another student's work.

After the activity, the class discusses other tools that help people read: a quiet seat, a line marker, or a clear copy without blurred letters. The teacher does not ask anyone to explain private reasons for using a particular aid.

The students compare answers by citing the story rather than the size of their pages. The discussion helps them focus on the learning goal. Different ways of accessing the same material need not mean that the thinking task has been changed.

Day 147 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Walk with a Gap in the Line

理解裝置紀錄缺漏與實際行程的差異。

After a family walk, Lio checks the route drawn by a phone app. Most of the path follows the river, but one section cuts straight across a block of buildings. He knows the family walked around those buildings on the public path and never crossed through them.

The app's signal was weak during that part of the trip. The displayed line connects two recorded points without showing every step between them. Lio first considers telling his friend that the app proved a shortcut exists, then compares the line with his own notes.

He marks the uncertain section and keeps the time-stamped photos taken before and after it. The total distance shown by the app may be affected by the missing route detail. He does not replace the number with a guess and call it a measurement.

When sharing the walk, Lio describes the path they actually used and notes the recording gap. A digital line can be a helpful record without being a perfect map of every movement. Checking it against other evidence makes the shared route more trustworthy.

Day 149 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Pebbles from the Top of the Jar

理解取樣位置與樣本偏差。

In a classroom sampling activity, a clear jar contains red and gray pebbles. Before the lesson, the teacher pours the red ones in last, leaving many near the top. The class does not know the exact total of either color and wants to estimate the mixture.

One group takes ten pebbles from the top and finds eight red ones. It concludes that about eighty percent of all pebbles are red. Another group notices that the upper layer may not represent the whole jar because the colors were not mixed.

The teacher lets students gently mix the jar, then select several small samples without looking for a preferred color. Each sample is recorded and returned before the next one is taken. The class compares how the sample results vary rather than treating one handful as certain.

The first handful remains a useful example of selection bias. It truly contained eight red pebbles, but the method favored a particular part of the jar. A correct count can still support an unreliable estimate if the sample is chosen poorly.

  3. The first group painted them.
  4. They are all larger than gray pebbles.

  1. Two pebbles in total.
  2. Ten red pebbles out of eight.
  3. Eight red pebbles out of ten.
  4. Eighty pebbles of each color.

Why might the estimate be unreliable?

  1. Taking only from the unmixed top favors red pebbles.
  2. Every sample must match the jar exactly.
  3. Percentages cannot describe colors.
  4. The count of eight was never made.

What does 'bias' mean here?

  1. The jar's empty space.
  2. A mistake in every addition.
  3. A systematic leaning caused by how the sample is selected.
  4. A perfectly representative whole-jar count.

5 · 資訊整合 · 進階

Which revised method addresses the main selection problem?

  1. Change gray pebbles to red before counting.
  2. Take only the reddest visible pebbles.
  3. Always select from the untouched top layer.
  4. Mix the jar and take several samples without choosing by color.

What can be true at the same time?

  1. Mixing eliminates the need to record samples.
  2. The top layer always represents every jar.
  3. The sample count is correct, so every population claim is certain.
  4. The sample count is correct and its whole-jar estimate is weak.

Day 150 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Quiet Museum Morning

辨識服務調整與一般入場规则的關係。

QUIET MORNING AT THE MUSEUM: On the first Sunday of each month, the museum reduces background music from nine to eleven. Some moving displays run without sound during that period. Visitors who prefer a calmer setting are welcome, but ordinary entry tickets are still required.

The session does not mean the building will be completely silent. People may speak softly, and the front doors will open and close as usual. A small rest room is available beside the map desk. Please ask staff before entering because its capacity is limited.

Book the quiet-morning time slot online. The booking reserves an arrival period, not a private room or a personal guide. If you need information about step-free routes, contact the desk before visiting. A route map can be sent in advance.

At eleven, the regular display sound resumes. Visitors already inside may remain until the normal closing time. They do not have to leave when the quiet period ends, but the reduced-sound conditions will no longer apply.

Day 151 · 每週 Boss · 15 分鐘

Boss: A Book for Each Reader

跨書目特徵與讀者需求做選擇。

BOOK CARDS: Harbor Secret is an illustrated mystery story with eighty pages. Animals Nearby is a factual guide with one hundred and twenty pages, maps, and animal photographs. Beyond the Clouds is a ninety-page factual space guide with no pictures. All three are available from the library.

READER NOTES: Jo wants fiction under one hundred pages with pictures. Ren wants factual information about local animals and does not mind a longer book. Lin wants a factual book under one hundred pages and is comfortable reading without illustrations.

GROUP REQUEST: The three first hope to borrow one title that satisfies all their needs. Their teacher asks them to compare the cards before assuming such a title exists. They may instead borrow separate books and share one interesting idea at next week's reading circle.

Jo selects Harbor Secret, Ren chooses Animals Nearby, and Lin takes Beyond the Clouds. Each writes which features supported the choice. A book can suit one reader without meeting another reader's current purpose, so the group does not label the unchosen titles bad.

Day 152 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Review of Small Qualifications

找出限定詞對句意與選項的影響。

Five review cards read delivered, bias, resumes, factual, and features. The teacher asks students to focus on small qualifications around each word. A statement may be accurate only within a certain stage, period, or group, so reading the noun alone is not enough.

A message can be delivered before the reader opens it. A sample may show bias if its selection favors one part of a jar. Regular sound resumes when a special quiet period ends. A factual book aims to provide information rather than an invented story.

For features, the class lists page count, pictures, and subject as characteristics that help choose a book. They then change one reader's requirement and check the choice again. The answer may change even though none of the book cards has changed.

Each pair writes a sentence beginning only if and another beginning even though. They explain how the added words limit or contrast the main idea. The review ends when students can support a choice with the whole condition, not just one attractive detail.

Day 153 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Club Name Nobody Understood

從讀者反應調整標示，區別熟悉與清楚。

The school opens a new room for fixing small household objects and learning simple craft skills. Club members call it the Spark Lab, a name they have used for months. Their opening poster says Visit the Spark Lab at lunch, but several younger students walk past without understanding what happens there.

Luan suggests adding a plain explanation under the name. Some members worry that explaining the familiar name will make the poster less exciting. Their teacher asks whether the intended visitors share the group's background knowledge. A name can feel obvious to insiders and still be unclear to others.

The revised poster reads Spark Lab: repair small objects, learn basic tools, and ask before borrowing equipment. It also lists the room number and opening days. Younger students begin asking specific questions about broken pencil cases and loose buttons instead of guessing whether the room teaches chemistry.

The members keep their name and add useful information. Luan learns that clarity need not remove personality: it helps readers connect an unfamiliar label with an action they understand.

Day 154 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Second Reminder at the Door

用位置與時機推論提醒效果。

After forgetting her reusable lunch box twice, Miki writes Bring the Box on a note above her bedroom desk. She sees it while doing homework, but by the time she leaves for school the next morning, the lunch box is still drying in the kitchen.

Her brother suggests moving the reminder to a place connected with the action. Miki puts a clean box beside her schoolbag each evening and leaves a small note on the bag's handle. The next morning, the note appears at the moment she is about to leave.

She still checks that the box is clean and closed rather than treating the note as proof that everything is ready. When the box is drying, she turns the note over to show Not packed yet. This makes the preparation status visible instead of relying on memory alone.

After a week, Miki has remembered the box each day. This does not prove the method works for everyone. Her reminder fits her own routine by linking the message, place, and time of action.

Day 155 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

A Joke Without a Face

從訊息語氣、回應與補充線索判斷人物意思。

[Class chat] Eva: My poster won the vote! Ben: Great. Another poster with a giant cat. Eva: If you hate it, you could have said so before the vote. Ben: Wait. I was smiling when I wrote that.

Eva: I couldn't see your smile. I spent three evenings drawing it. Ben: I meant that everyone knows I love cats. But you joined our class last month, so you wouldn't know that. I'm sorry my message sounded unkind.

Eva: Thanks for explaining. Maybe add what you actually like about it? Ben: The bright background makes the meeting date easy to find. Also, the cat looks as if it wants to join our club.

After the exchange, Ben edits his first message to include a clear compliment. He does not tell Eva to become less sensitive. Instead, he notices that a shared screen does not mean shared knowledge. Their next conversation is easier because both explain what the other person could not see.

Day 156 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Damp Patch on the Wall

分辨觀察、可能原因與能區分假設的後續檢查。

After a rainy weekend, a class notices a damp patch on the wall beside its fish tank. Owen says the roof must be leaking because it rained. Priya points out that someone also changed the tank water on Friday.

The teacher writes two possible explanations on the board. Rainwater may have entered through the roof, or spilled tank water may have wet the wall. The patch alone cannot tell the class which explanation is correct.

Students ask the caretaker to inspect the area safely. They also check the water-changing record and photographs from Friday. One photograph shows a dry wall after the tank was cleaned. That makes an earlier spill less likely, although it does not explain every possible source of moisture.

The class keeps both observations and remaining questions in its report. Owen changes 'The rain caused it' to 'A roof leak needs further checking.' He has not discovered the final cause yet, but his sentence now matches the strength of the evidence.

Day 157 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Student Voices: Recording Invitation

整合錄音活動的參與、同意與公開使用條件。

STUDENT VOICES PROJECT: The school radio team invites students to record a two-minute story about a place they enjoy. Recording sessions take place in Room 204 on Wednesday after class. You may bring a written script, but reading from one is optional.

Recording and broadcasting are separate choices. At the session, choose 'practice only' or 'consider for broadcast.' Practice recordings stay with the student and are not added to the radio team's collection. Choosing broadcast consideration does not guarantee that your story will be selected.

If selected, you will receive an edited version to review. The team will broadcast it only after you approve that version. You may request changes or decline without giving a reason. Silence does not count as approval.

Stories may use a first name or an invented name. Please leave out other people's private details. If a recording mentions someone who could easily be recognized, the team will discuss changes with the speaker before any broadcast.

Day 158 · 每週 Boss · 15 分鐘

Boss: Three Versions of the Same Interview

跨文本比較原話、節錄與標題是否保留原意。

[Interview] Reporter: Will the reading room open every evening? Principal: We hope to try that next month, but only if we can find enough adult helpers. At present, the room closes at five. We will announce a decision next Friday.

[Student article draft] The school hopes to test evening opening next month. The plan depends on finding adult helpers, and no final decision has been made. Until a change is announced, the five o'clock closing time remains in place.

[Poster draft] GOOD NEWS! Reading room open every evening from next month. Stay as long as you want! A student designer says the short headline will attract more readers than a sentence full of conditions.

The editor checks both drafts against the interview. She keeps the article but returns the poster for revision. An attractive message still needs to represent what was said. She suggests 'Evening opening under consideration' and adds the date of the coming announcement below it.

Day 159 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Words That Changed the Message

複習語氣、假設及同意條件，找出改寫遺失的限制。

At the review table, Hana receives five words from recent readings: compliment, damp, optional, approve, and consideration. Instead of matching them to isolated definitions, she must repair short messages that have lost important information.

The first message calls Ben's friendly praise a complaint. Hana replaces that word with compliment. Next, a wall report says that a damp patch proves a roof leak. She keeps damp but changes 'proves' to 'may suggest,' because other causes were possible.

A radio invitation says every speaker needs a script and every recording will be broadcast. Hana writes that scripts are optional and speakers must approve the selected edited recording. Merely joining a session does not give permission for every later use.

Finally, a poster turns a plan under consideration into a promise. Hana restores the missing condition about helpers. Her teacher asks which correction matters most. Hana says each one repairs a different gap: tone, evidence, choice, permission, or certainty. Knowing the words helps only when she also checks their relationships.

Day 160 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Part No One Applauded

由敘事細節推論人物價值觀與態度轉變。

At the school play, the loudest applause goes to the students on stage. Backstage, Jun folds costumes while watching the actors receive flowers. He has spent weeks checking buttons and repairing pockets, but his name appears near the bottom of the program.

When an actor thanks him for fixing a loose sleeve just before the performance, Jun smiles briefly. He still wishes the audience had seen what he did. He starts to leave the empty dressing room without taking a group photograph.

Then the director asks everyone to gather around the costume table. She describes how the repaired sleeve allowed an actor to move freely and how clearly labeled clothes prevented mistakes. Her thanks are specific, rather than a quick mention of 'all the helpers.'

Jun joins the photograph. The applause from earlier has not changed, and he has not suddenly become an actor. What changes is his sense that his work was understood. On the way home, he keeps the program instead of throwing it into a recycling bin.

Day 161 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Last Piece of Cake

比較人物表面行動、未說出的期待與溝通結果。

At dinner, Aunt May asks whether anyone wants the last piece of cake. Leo says, 'I'm fine,' because he expects someone to offer it a second time. His cousin Nina hears a refusal and puts the cake on her own plate.

Leo becomes quiet. Later, he tells his mother that Nina was selfish. His mother asks what Nina actually heard. Leo repeats his words and realizes that he never said he wanted the cake. In Nina's home, people usually accept the first answer.

The next evening, Nina offers him a peach. Leo says, 'Yes, please. I would like half if you want some too.' Nina happily shares it. Neither needs to guess whether a polite phrase hides a different wish.

Leo still enjoys offering food to others before serving himself. He does not decide that one family's habit is wrong. Instead, he learns to explain his wishes when different habits meet. The missing cake becomes a small lesson about asking what someone meant before judging their character.

Day 162 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

Which River Photo Is Ours?

[Project chat] Sara: I found a beautiful river photo for our local history page. The file is called River_New. Mo: Is that our river? The bridge looks different. Sara: It came from the folder our group shared yesterday.

Mo: That folder includes examples from other towns. Can you open the original page? Sara: You're right. This picture shows a town far away. I assumed everything in the shared folder was local. Mo: The filename doesn't tell us where a picture was taken.

Sara: I also found an old photograph in the town museum's collection. Its description names our bridge and gives the year. We can ask about using it and keep that information beside the image. Mo: Good. Let's check the caption as carefully as the picture.

The group replaces the attractive but unrelated photograph. Their page now uses a less colorful image that actually supports the local story. They add source notes so the next editor can trace each picture without relying on a folder name.

Day 163 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Shade That Moved

依觀察時間理解測量結果的適用範圍。

For a school garden project, students draw a map of sunny and shaded spaces at nine in the morning. They mark the corner beside the library as shaded and choose it for a reading bench. The map looks complete until they return after lunch.

At one o'clock, the same corner is bright, while part of the opposite path is shaded. The students realize that a label without a time can mislead a reader. Their first map described one visit, not a permanent condition.

They observe the area again at several times on two more school days and record both the time and weather. They do not claim that these visits describe every season. Instead, they use the observations to discuss when students are most likely to sit outside.

The revised proposal includes separate morning and afternoon maps. It recommends checking conditions during the planned reading period before fixing the bench in place. The project changes from finding a spot called 'shaded' to finding a spot suitable for a particular use.

Day 164 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

A Free Trial with a Return Date

閱讀借用體驗公告，區分免費使用與贈送。

TRY A MUSICAL INSTRUMENT: The community music room is offering a free seven-day trial of selected instruments. The offer covers borrowing an instrument, not private lessons. A staff member will show you how to carry and store it before you leave.

Bring a student card and an adult contact number. Each borrower may choose one instrument that is currently available. A waiting list is used when all instruments of a kind are out. Joining the list does not start your seven-day period.

The return date is printed on your receipt when you collect the instrument. Return it during staffed hours, Tuesday to Saturday, from two to six. Please contact the music room before the due date if a problem prevents your return.

The trial is a chance to explore an interest without buying equipment first. The instrument remains the music room's property. Do not pass it to another borrower yourself, even if that person is next on the waiting list; staff must check and record every return.

Labels That Need Their Partners

Five cards lie on Tessa's review desk: caption, permanent, trial, property, and departure. Each card belongs beside a sentence that is almost correct. Tessa's job is to notice the missing partner: a source, a time, a limit, an owner, or a location.

A river picture has a caption saying 'our town,' but its original source names another town. Tessa changes the caption. A garden map calls a morning patch of shade permanent. She adds the observation time instead of promising shade all day.

A music notice describes a free trial as a gift. Tessa writes that the instrument remains the music room's property and must be returned. She also checks when staff are available, because knowing an item must be returned is not enough to plan a visit.

The final card says the club bus has a new departure time. Tessa remembers that only its gate changed. She corrects the location and keeps 9:10. The exercise reminds her that a familiar word can still lead to a wrong answer when it is attached to the wrong detail.

Day 167 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Empty Chair in the Debate

比較辯論立場，推論缺席觀點及合理協商方式。

The student council debates whether to replace a quiet courtyard with a game area. Several speakers say the courtyard looks empty at lunchtime, so it must be wasted space. Most students in the meeting are members of sports or performance clubs.

A quiet student named Bo asks when the speakers visited. He goes there before class to read and after lunch to rest from noise. Another student uses the courtyard to talk privately with a friend. Neither usually attends council meetings.

The chairperson places an empty chair beside the speakers and labels it 'people we have not asked.' Before voting, the council posts a short survey at the courtyard and invites students with different routines to comment. The empty chair is a reminder, not a vote.

The final proposal keeps a quiet corner and tests a small game area at specified times. The council has not made everyone want the same thing. It has improved the decision by noticing whose experience was missing from the first discussion.

Day 168 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

A Gift with an Unfinished Story

從人物回憶推論物品的情感意義與故事主旨。

For his grandfather's birthday, Ken plans to buy a new watch. His grandfather's old one has a scratched face and a faded strap. Ken thinks a shiny replacement will be an obvious improvement, so he asks what color his grandfather would like.

His grandfather turns the old watch over. On the back is a short message from Ken's grandmother, written many years ago. The watch stopped working last winter, but he still wears it because the message makes him feel close to her.

Ken changes his plan. With his grandfather's agreement, he takes the watch to a repair shop and asks what can be repaired without removing the message. The shop can replace a small part inside while keeping the original back.

On the birthday, Ken returns the working watch with a card describing what he learned. His grandfather checks the time, then turns it over again. Ken understands that a useful gift begins with attention to the person receiving it. Newness was his first idea of value, but it was not his grandfather's.

The Reply Sent to the Wrong Group

[Drama group] Mei: Please bring your blue shirt on Friday. We need it for the final scene. Aaron: Done. I sent the reminder to everyone. [Science group, five minutes later] Aaron: Sorry, the blue-shirt message was meant for the drama group.

Back in the drama chat, Mei asks whether the correct group received the reminder. Aaron checks and discovers that he never sent it there. He posts it, names Friday's performance, and asks members to react after reading so he can check who still needs the information.

Sending a correction to the wrong audience would not have solved the whole problem. Aaron needed to remove confusion in one group and deliver the missing instruction to another. He changes the two chat icons so their similar names are easier to tell apart.

Day 170 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

How Much Water Left the Cup?

比較測量精度，分辨相同讀數與完全相同的量。

In a classroom activity, two groups measure water in small cups. Group A uses a jug with marks every ten milliliters. Group B uses a narrow measuring cylinder with marks every milliliter. Both groups report that their cups contain about thirty milliliters.

Yuri says the amounts must be exactly equal because the written numbers match. His partner points to the different scales. The jug cannot show small differences as clearly as the cylinder. The same rounded report can hide differences between actual amounts.

The teacher asks the groups to describe their tools beside their results. She also reminds them to view the liquid level consistently. A tool with smaller marks can help, but careless reading can still introduce error.

The students revise their claim to say that both readings are near thirty milliliters within the limits of their methods. They have not made their work less useful by mentioning limits. They have made it easier for another reader to understand what the numbers can, and cannot, establish.

Day 171 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Borrow a Board Game, Keep the Pieces Together

整合借用清單、缺件通報與歸還程序。

BOARD GAME BORROWING DESK: Students may borrow one game for up to three school days. The box contains a piece list and a return card. Before leaving, compare the contents with the list and tell the desk helper about anything already missing.

The helper will note existing missing pieces on the return card. This record prevents the next borrower from being blamed for an earlier problem. Do not assume that a closed box has been checked; returned games may be waiting for inspection.

If a piece disappears during your loan, report it when returning the game. A clear report is more helpful than replacing it with an object that may confuse the next players. Staff will decide how to repair the set.

Games must be returned to the desk, not placed directly on the borrowing shelf. A game marked 'under inspection' is unavailable even when its box is visible. Ask the helper to recommend another game while you wait for the checked set to return.

Day 172 · 每週 Boss · 15 分鐘

Boss: The Missing Page in the Report

結合調查方法、數據與提案，評估主張是否合理。

[Survey summary] The art club asked twenty students leaving its exhibition whether the school should hold more art events. Sixteen said yes, three said no, and one was unsure. The club's draft report states, 'Eighty percent of all students want more art events.'

[Method note] Students were questioned only at the exhibition exit between three and four. No students who stayed away from the exhibition were contacted. The school has four hundred students. The report's missing second page contains these details.

[Council response] The result tells us about these twenty visitors. It does not establish the views of the whole school. Please include the method page and seek responses from students with different activities before making a school-wide claim.

The art club keeps the original numbers but changes its wording. It proposes one small trial event while collecting broader feedback. Its members learn that a limited survey can still be useful when the group described by the conclusion matches the group actually questioned.

Day 173 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Review with Two Columns

複習誤傳、量測、檢查與調查範圍的閱讀線索。

Rui draws two columns headed 'What the text says' and 'What I added.' He uses five recent words to check his reading: mistaken, rounded, inspection, broader, and conclusion. His teacher asks him to place each claim in the correct column.

Rui first writes that a mistaken shirt reminder created a science dress rule. Then he notices the correction and moves his claim to the second column. He also removes the idea that two rounded water readings prove exactly equal amounts.

A visible game box seems ready to borrow, but its inspection label says otherwise. Rui keeps the label's information in the first column. From the art survey, he records sixteen yes answers among twenty visitors and leaves out a claim about all four hundred students.

To form a broader conclusion, he would need information from a wider range of students. Rui realizes that his second column is not a list of foolish ideas. It is a place to notice assumptions and ask which ones have support before using them as answers.

The Apology on the Noticeboard

由補救行動判斷道歉的誠意與敘事重點。

When a class poster disappears, Mina tells two friends that she thinks Sam took it. She has seen him near the noticeboard, but she has not asked him anything. By lunch, several classmates are repeating the claim as if it were a fact.

The teacher later finds the poster in a storage drawer. A helper had moved it while cleaning the board. Mina apologizes to Sam in a private message. Sam replies, 'Thank you, but the others still think I took it.'

Mina realizes that a private apology has not corrected a public misunderstanding. With Sam's agreement, she tells the classmates who heard her claim what actually happened. She says clearly that she had no evidence Sam removed the poster.

Some friends tell her to stop mentioning an embarrassing mistake. Mina answers that she is not repeating the rumor; she is correcting it. Sam does not immediately become cheerful, but the next day he asks her to help put the poster back. Trust begins to return through a concrete action.

Day 175 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Bag Left Beside the Register

整合視角與行動，避免以片段觀察判定動機。

In a small grocery shop, Wei sees a customer leave a full shopping bag beside the register and walk outside. The cashier does not call after her. Wei wonders whether the customer has forgotten the bag or left without paying.

He starts to warn the cashier, who explains that the customer has already paid. She is bringing her bicycle from the rack so the heavy bag can be placed directly in its basket. They agreed on this before Wei entered the shop.

A minute later, the customer returns with the bicycle. The cashier helps lift the bag, and the customer thanks her. Wei notices that the scene looks different once he knows the earlier conversation. His observation was accurate, but his possible explanations were incomplete.

On the walk home, he remembers that he asked instead of accusing anyone. He does not conclude that every strange situation has a harmless explanation. He learns to describe what he saw, keep possibilities separate from facts, and seek missing information before making a confident judgment.

Day 176 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

Don't Tell Me How It Ends

從讀者回應推論訊息應保留及省略的內容。

[Book club chat] Dani: Is The Red Door worth reading? Please don't reveal the ending. Sol: Yes! The part where the missing brother returns is amazing. Dani: I was only on chapter two. I didn't know he was alive.

Sol: I'm sorry. I thought you meant not to reveal the final sentence. Dani: I meant information that would remove the surprise. You could tell me about the writing or the kinds of questions the story raises without answering them.

Sol removes the detail from his recommendation for other readers. He writes, 'The story gradually changes how we understand the family. Small objects mentioned early become important later.' He labels a separate discussion thread 'Finished readers only' before posting details about the ending there.

Dani continues reading, although one surprise has been spoiled. At their next meeting, Sol asks how far each person has read before discussing the plot. He learns that an accurate description can still be unsuitable when the reader has asked for a particular limit.

Day 177 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Answer Box That Looked Too Small

比較作答版面、回答長度與內容品質，辨識可能影響。

In a fictional classroom activity, two groups receive the same prompt: describe the school garden. One sheet provides two lines for an answer, while the other provides half a page. Neither gives a word limit. The teacher wants to explore whether the space offered may affect responses.

Students using the larger box generally write more, but their answers vary. Some add useful observations, while others repeat a point. The class separates answer length from the amount of information. More words do not automatically mean a better description.

After discussing the setup, students ask whether the groups already differed in writing habits or garden knowledge. They suggest a follow-up with neutral wording and a more careful comparison of the writers. The activity raises a question about presentation; it does not prove that a larger box improves every answer or that every short response lacks detail.

SMALL STORY COMPETITION: Write an original fictional story of 120 to 180 words. Entries must be in English and submitted by one student, not a team. Give your story a title; the title does not count toward the word limit.

Submit through the school form by five on Friday. A saved draft is not an entry. Press 'Submit' and check for a confirmation number. If no number appears, ask the library desk for help before the deadline.

What the Confirmation Cannot Promise

During review, Lila circles five words: reveal, neutral, revise, excluding, and confirmation. She notices that several recent passages warn readers against giving a word more power than it has. A confirmation number, for example, says a form arrived; it does not announce a prize.

Her first task is to recommend a mystery without revealing its surprise. She describes the writing and leaves the answer to the mystery untouched. For the answer-box activity, she chooses neutral wording that does not tell students whether to praise or criticize the garden.

Next, she helps a fictional student revise a story. The body contains 182 words, excluding a three-word title. Lila says at least two body words must go to reach a 180-word limit. Deleting only the title would not solve the problem.

She finishes by checking whether the revised entry was actually submitted. A good edit saved on a computer may never reach the judges. Lila's review rule is simple: after understanding a sentence, ask exactly what it establishes and what still requires another action or piece of evidence.

Day 181 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Tutor Who Asked One More Question

由教學互動推論人物策略及學習成效的證據。

During peer tutoring, Neil points to a reading question and asks his partner, Ada, for the answer. Ada sees the correct option immediately, but she asks, 'Which sentence made you choose yours?' Neil shrugs and says the option contains a word from the passage.

Ada asks him to read the whole sentence around that word. It says the club considered a picnic but chose an indoor visit because of rain. Neil's option names the picnic, which appears in the text but is not the final plan.

Together they underline 'considered' and 'but chose.' Ada then gives Neil a different short example in which a family first discusses a train and finally takes a bus. This time, he identifies the chosen transport and explains the contrast without help.

Neil leaves with one corrected answer and a method he can try again. Ada has not made him finish the entire worksheet faster. She has helped him notice the relationship between ideas, so a familiar word is less likely to pull him toward the wrong option.

Day 182 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Postcard That Took the Long Way

追蹤時間線，推論實體物件與即時訊息的不同意義。

On a weekend trip, Iona sends her grandmother a postcard with a drawing of the coast. She also sends a phone photograph that evening. Her grandmother replies to the photograph at once, so Iona wonders whether the postcard was unnecessary.

The postcard arrives nine days later, after Iona is already home. Her grandmother places it beside a much older card from Iona's first school trip. The two drawings show the same sea in very different ways, and the handwriting has changed too.

When Iona visits, they compare the cards. The older message says only that the bus ride was fun. The new one describes a quiet moment watching fishing boats return. Her grandmother says she enjoys seeing not just where Iona went, but what she noticed.

Iona still sends quick photographs when she travels. She also understands why a slower message can matter. The postcard did not compete with the phone for speed; it became something they could hold, keep, and revisit together long after the immediate news was known.

Day 183 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

A Photo for the Group Page

辨識不同用途的同意範圍並追蹤修改方案。

[Volunteer chat] Kim: I took a group photograph after our cleanup. May I send it here? Everyone: Yes. Kim: Great. I'll also put it on the public project page. Rena: I agreed to this private group, but not to a public page.

Kim: Thanks for telling me. I thought one yes covered both places. Rena: Could the public page show our collected materials instead? I am happy for people to see the work. I just don't want my face posted there.

Kim checks with the other volunteers and takes a new photograph of the sorted materials without anyone in view. She writes a caption thanking the whole team without listing personal details. The group photograph stays in the private chat as originally agreed.

At the next event, Kim asks two separate questions before taking pictures: who is comfortable being photographed, and where each picture may be shared. She learns that respecting a limit does not prevent a project from telling its story; it changes which picture tells that story.

Day 184 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Silent Scene Experiment

比較相同畫面下不同背景資訊對解讀的影響。

A media class watches a silent ten-second clip of a boy waiting beside a door. Before showing it, the teacher tells half the class that the boy is waiting for an exam result. The other half hears that he is waiting for a surprise birthday guest.

The first group often describes him as nervous. The second often calls him excited. Both groups saw the same clip, and the actor had been asked only to stand and look toward the door. The stories supplied beforehand shaped many interpretations.

Some students in each group choose different words, so the teacher avoids saying that background information controls every viewer. The class compares reports and marks which details were visible and which came from the introduction.

For their next film review, students plan to describe gestures before naming emotions. They can still make an interpretation, but they should explain its basis and consider alternatives. The activity shows how a small piece of surrounding information can change the story a viewer builds from an unchanged image.

Listen to the Old Street

整合導覽使用方式、替代閱讀及路線安全條件。

OLD STREET AUDIO WALK: Explore six marked stops with short recordings about local shops and buildings. You may follow the stops in any order. Scan the code on each marker; downloading all recordings at the visitor desk before starting is another option.

The complete walk takes about forty minutes, including listening and walking. If you have less time, choose individual stops. A printed transcript is available free at the desk and contains the same stories. Bringing headphones is recommended, but listening aloud near homes is not allowed.

Stop 4 stands across a busy road. Use the marked crossing even if another route looks shorter. The recording is designed to be heard while standing beside the marker, not while crossing.

The visitor desk closes at five, but the outdoor markers remain accessible. Borrowed audio players must be returned by 4:45. Visitors using their own phones and downloaded recordings may finish later. Please respect residents and keep doorways clear throughout your visit.

Boss: A Shorter Old Street Visit

[Visit rules] Old Street has six audio stops. Visitors may choose any stops. Printed transcripts tell the same stories. Borrowed players must return to the desk by 4:45; downloaded recordings on personal phones have no equipment return deadline.

[Time estimates] From the desk, a visit to Stops 1 and 2 and back takes twenty minutes, including both recordings. Stops 3 and 4 and back take thirty minutes. All six stops and the return take forty minutes. These are complete route times, not times for each stop.

The Condition Under the Main Sentence

複習同意範圍、解讀與時間餘裕，找出關鍵條件。

Jin's review sheet uses five words from the week: public, interpretations, transcript, margin, and condition. A large sentence appears at the top of each card, while a smaller line below it adds information. Jin must read both before deciding what action is reasonable.

One card says a group approved a photograph. The smaller line says approval was for a private chat. Jin rejects a plan to post it publicly. Another card describes a boy as nervous; its lower line reveals that viewers heard an exam story before watching.

A walking-tour card says the route takes thirty minutes. Below it, the borrower arrives at 4:15, must return a player at 4:45, and wants a ten-minute margin. Jin explains that finishing on time would still fail that preference.

For a visitor who wants the stories without audio, Jin selects a transcript. He notices that the smaller lines are not always unimportant details. A condition can change which answer is best, even when the largest sentence on the page remains completely true.

Day 188 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

A Different Kind of Team Captain

根據連續行動推論領導方式與人物成長。

When the class chooses a captain for its puzzle race, everyone expects loud, quick-speaking Rex to lead. Instead, the teacher asks quiet Nori to try. Rex looks disappointed and says the team may waste time if nobody gives immediate orders.

At the first station, Nori asks each member what they notice. One sees a number pattern, another spots a word hidden in the instructions, and Rex finds a shortcut between two clues. Nori repeats the ideas clearly and asks which ones can be checked.

The team loses a minute testing a wrong pattern, then corrects it because someone feels comfortable pointing out the mistake. Nori thanks that student instead of defending the first idea. Rex begins asking questions too, and the last station goes smoothly.

They finish second. On the way back, Rex says winning would have been nice, but he had not expected so many useful ideas to come from listening. Nori smiles and asks him to lead the next practice using the same approach. The captain's job, they discover, can be to make other people's thinking visible.

Day 189 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Umbrella with the Bright Patch

從人物對物品的態度變化理解對比與象徵。

Lena's umbrella develops a small tear just before a week of rain. She wants to replace it, but her older brother offers to sew on a waterproof patch from his repair kit. The only patch he has is bright yellow, while the umbrella is dark blue.

Lena worries that the repair will look strange. She agrees to try it because the frame and handle are still sound. Her brother explains what he can fix, and they test the repaired area with water before she carries it outside.

At school, a friend says the yellow shape looks like a little sun. Later, when several blue umbrellas crowd the stand, Lena finds hers immediately. The mark she wanted to hide has become both useful and personal.

She does not decide that every broken object should always be repaired. This umbrella had a small problem that the available method could solve. By Friday, she is no longer comparing it with a perfect new one. She likes the story of its repair and the bright shape that made it hers.

Day 190 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

Whose Words Are in the Review?

區分直接引語、改寫與群體立場的歸屬。

[Review team] Tess: I wrote, 'Everyone found the play confusing.' Is that fair? Omar: I said the opening scene was confusing, but the ending helped me understand it. Pia: I enjoyed it throughout. Please don't turn one comment into the whole group's opinion.

Tess: I'll write that some viewers needed time to understand the opening. Omar: Can you say that this was my experience? We only asked three people. Pia: And if you quote me, use my actual words. A summary is fine, but it shouldn't look like an exact quotation.

Tess revises the review. She attributes the opening-scene comment to Omar, includes Pia's different reaction, and marks her own summary clearly. The piece now contains disagreement without becoming untidy. Its readers can tell who said what and how much the report supports. Tess learns that making a group sound united can remove information readers need.

Day 191 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Fast Sorting, Careful Sorting

結合完成時間與錯誤數判讀活動表現。

In a classroom investigation, pairs sort picture cards into four groups. In the first round, they are told to finish as fast as possible. In the second, they are told to check every card before stopping. Each round uses a different set with the same number of cards.

One pair finishes the first round in forty seconds with five mistakes. Their second round takes seventy seconds with one mistake. Jun calls the first result better because it is faster. His partner asks whether speed alone is the goal.

The class reports both time and errors. They also note that the second set may have been easier or harder, and practice from the first round may have helped. Their results describe what happened under these conditions. A further comparison could vary the order between groups to examine the instructions more fairly.

The Saturday Skill Exchange

閱讀技能交換規則，分辨點數用途與參與條件。

SATURDAY SKILL EXCHANGE: Teach a short skill and learn another. Each approved fifteen-minute teaching session earns one learning credit after it is completed. Offering a session on the sign-up sheet does not earn credit immediately. The coordinator must confirm that it took place.

One credit books one learning session, regardless of the number of minutes you previously spent preparing. Credits cannot be exchanged for cash or transferred to another person. You may attend several sessions if you have enough credits and the times do not overlap.

New participants receive one starter credit so they can try learning before teaching. Unused credits remain available for next month's exchange. If a teacher cancels a booked session, the learner's credit is returned. Please check the updated timetable on Friday; the list printed earlier in the week may no longer show the final rooms.

Day 194 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

From One Comment to a Whole Claim

複習來源歸屬、誤差與資格，練習限制推論範圍。

At the weekly review, Sia receives five words: quotation, errors, overlap, confirmed, and current. Her task is to explain why an answer that sounds reasonable may still go beyond a passage. She begins with a review that makes three viewers sound like an entire audience.

Sia marks a quotation only when it uses a speaker's actual words. She keeps Omar's reaction separate from Pia's. In the sorting activity, she reports both speed and errors, because choosing only one measurement hides part of the performance.

For the skill exchange, she counts a starter credit and one confirmed teaching session. A future offer does not increase the current total. She also checks whether two selected sessions overlap instead of assuming that enough credits guarantee a workable schedule.

Sia writes her own reminder at the bottom: 'Check the source, the measurement, and the rule that connects facts to an answer.' These questions take a little time, but they help her avoid turning a partial truth into an unsupported conclusion.

The Plant with Two Watering Signs

The teacher asks the class to compare the plans rather than blame either student first. They choose one shared record beside the window and write the date of each update on it. The next helper can now see both who is responsible and what has already been done.

Four Servings and a Smaller Bowl

Aron finds a fruit-salad recipe that serves four. It calls for two apples, two bananas, and one cup of yogurt. Only Aron and his sister will eat it, so he decides to prepare half the recipe rather than store two extra servings.

He writes a new list with one apple, one banana, and half a cup of yogurt. His sister points out that they have small bowls. Aron says the number of bowls does not change the ingredient ratio; they can divide the mixture between bowls after making it.

The printed amount is a guide for that recipe, not a requirement to empty a container. Aron measures a half-cup portion but adds it in stages. The two follow both the scaled quantities and the writer's instruction about checking the result.

Day 198 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Timer That Started at Three

區分顯示讀數與經過時間，依共同起訖點比較。

During a classroom race between toy cars, students use a large timer that has not been reset. It shows three seconds when the first car starts and thirteen when that car finishes. Pat records thirteen seconds as the car's travel time.

His partner points out that the car did not begin at zero. They subtract the starting reading from the finishing reading and record ten seconds instead. For the second car, the readings are twenty and thirty-two, giving twelve seconds of travel.

The class compares durations rather than the final numbers on the screen. Both cars traveled the same marked distance, and each start was recorded at the line. The students still note that pressing a button by hand introduces some uncertainty. A correct subtraction fixes Pat's calculation, but it does not make the timing method perfect or support conclusions about every toy car.
