Twenty Minutes of Actual Reading

區分閱讀活動時長、休息時間與徽章取得條件。

READING HABIT CHALLENGE: Earn a weekly badge by recording at least twenty minutes of reading on each of three different days. You may divide a day's reading into shorter periods. Minutes from different days cannot be combined to meet one day's target.

Pause your timer during breaks, including time spent choosing a new book. The challenge counts active reading time, not the total time you remain in the library. Write the book title and one idea you understood after each reading period.

The badge celebrates participation, not reading speed or an exam score. A difficult page may take longer than an easy one. If you miss a target day, keep your record and try again on another day within the same week. Do not replace an honest entry with an invented one just to complete the badge.

Day 200 · 每週 Boss · 15 分鐘

Boss: Reading Time and Library Time

整合閱讀紀錄、休息及每日門檻，辨識徽章意義。

[Challenge rule] A badge requires at least twenty active reading minutes on each of three different days in one week. Short periods on the same day may be added. Breaks and book selection do not count, and surplus minutes cannot be moved to another day.

[Mara's log] Monday: twelve minutes before class and nine afterward. Tuesday: thirty minutes in the library, including eight minutes choosing books and four minutes chatting. Thursday: twenty-five minutes of reading. Friday: twenty minutes of reading.

[Mara's comment] I spent the longest library period there on Tuesday, so that must be my strongest day. [Teacher] Library time and active reading time are different. Count the relevant minutes before judging whether the target was reached.

Mara checks the entries and keeps all of them, including the day below target. Her badge records consistent participation across enough days. It does not show that she reads faster than classmates, understands every page, or can predict a future exam result from minutes alone.

Day 201 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

A Number Needs Its Definition

複習時間界限、相減及有效閱讀，核對數字代表的量。

Five words guide Jo's review: boundary, subtract, durations, active, and surplus. She writes a number beside each word and then explains what that number represents. Her teacher says the explanation matters more than producing a long list of correct-looking figures.

For the volunteer message, four o'clock is a boundary on available help, not a new starting time. For the toy car, Jo must subtract the starting timer reading from the finishing reading to compare durations. A final display of thirteen does not mean thirteen seconds of travel.

In the reading challenge, thirty minutes inside a library may contain fewer active reading minutes. Jo removes breaks before checking the daily target. She also keeps surplus minutes on their actual day rather than moving them to another. The review helps her see that arithmetic works only after she identifies the quantity, its limits, and the rule under which it is being counted.

Day 202 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Story Behind an Unfinished Model

依人物行動推論未完成作品的意義與評量重點。

At the class exhibition, Mira places an unfinished bridge model beside two broken earlier versions. Other students display polished models on clean tables. Her friend worries that visitors will think she did less work because one side of her bridge is still open.

Mira adds a notebook showing where each version failed and what she changed. One early bridge bent at its center; the next held more weight but used too much material for the project limit. Her final design is lighter, though she has not completed every connection.

A visitor spends several minutes reading the notebook and asks why Mira moved a support. Mira can explain the evidence behind the change. She still needs to finish the model, but the exhibition reveals work that a finished surface alone would hide. Her teacher praises the clear record of decisions and sets a later check for completing the remaining construction.

Day 203 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Shortcut Through a Memory

比較熟悉記憶與現場資訊，推論改變決策的原因。

On a visit to his old neighborhood, Dan tells his younger sister that he knows a shortcut to the park. He used it every afternoon as a child. They follow the familiar lane until a new fence blocks the path behind an apartment building.

Dan feels certain there must be an opening farther along. His sister points to a sign directing visitors to the public entrance on the next street. She asks whether his memory describes the neighborhood now or the one he knew years ago.

They take the signed route and arrive a few minutes later. From the park, Dan can still see the tree beside his old shortcut, but the surrounding buildings have changed. He tells his sister a story about the tree while accepting that his remembered route is no longer available. His memory remains meaningful without being a reliable guide to every present detail.

Day 204 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

Does 'Maybe' Mean We Decided?

區分建議、討論與正式決定，追蹤對話共識。

[Class trip chat] Bea: Maybe we could eat near the station after the museum. Hugo: Good idea. I'll tell the restaurant we're coming. Lin: Have we chosen a place or checked who can stay? I thought Bea was suggesting an option.

Bea: That's right. My train leaves early, so I may not even join dinner. Hugo: I took 'good idea' as a decision. Lin: We still need a head count, a time, and agreement on a place before making a booking.

Hugo drafts a short poll instead of contacting a restaurant immediately. The group separates discussion from confirmation: ideas go in the chat, while final plans appear in a pinned message with the person responsible for each next step. By the end of the afternoon, they have a clear process, even though the dinner itself is not yet arranged. Nobody has to undo a booking made on an assumption.

Day 205 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Counting the Same Model Bird Twice

依觀察單位判斷數量，區分目擊次數與不同個體。

For an observation lesson, a teacher places eight model birds around a garden and asks two groups to count them from different paths. Group A records six sightings, and Group B records five. A student adds the numbers and announces eleven birds.

The teacher asks whether the groups might have seen some of the same models. Each bird carries a small colored tag. Comparing notes shows that three tagged birds appear in both lists. The class combines the lists and counts each tag only once.

The total is eight different models, although there were eleven recorded sightings. The teacher keeps both numbers and labels them clearly. One describes observations; the other describes distinct objects. Before a later outdoor survey, students discuss how much harder it would be to recognize untagged moving birds. The model activity gives them a counting question to consider, not a guarantee that real field observations will be equally simple.

The Museum's Fictional Missing Key

閱讀遊戲公告，辨識虛構情境及尋找線索的規則。

MUSEUM MYSTERY AFTERNOON: Help solve a fictional story about a missing key. This is a paper-based game; no real museum key has disappeared. Collect a clue booklet at the entrance and read the four character statements printed inside.

All information needed for the answer is in the booklet. Display cases and staff-only rooms are not part of the game, and nothing needs to be opened or moved. You may discuss ideas with other players, but submit one answer sheet per team.

Your answer should name a location and cite two clues that support it. A lucky guess without an explanation will not earn a completion stamp. If you need help, ask for a hint card; it points to a useful statement without giving the answer. Return the pencil afterward, but keep the booklet so you can explain your reasoning to someone at home.

Day 207 · 每週 Boss · 15 分鐘

Boss: Where the Story's Key Was Left

交叉比對明確線索與不確定回憶，排除不符地點。

[Game setup] A fictional key was left in one of four places: the reading room, the garden bench, the ticket desk, or the storage room. The booklet states that the key's final location is dry, open to visitors, and contains a clock.

[Place guide] The reading room is indoors, open to visitors, and has a wall clock. The garden bench is wet from rain and has no clock. The ticket desk is indoors and public but has no clock. The storage room is dry and has a clock, but visitors may not enter.

[Character notes] Al recalls carrying the key toward the ticket desk earlier. Bea saw Al later holding it near the reading-room door. Neither statement says where it was finally left. The location conditions in the setup are reliable facts for this game.

The team must choose one location and explain its answer using the conditions. An earlier movement can be interesting without settling the final location. The strongest answer must fit all three stated requirements, not just one memorable detail.

Day 208 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

All Three Clues Must Fit

複習假設、計數單位與線索條件，檢查答案完整性。

Rafi reviews five words: assumption, distinct, cite, location, and requirements. His first card contains a dinner suggestion followed by an immediate booking. He identifies the assumption that a positive reaction had already settled the place, time, and guests.

The second card lists eleven sightings of tagged model birds. Rafi compares the tags and finds only eight distinct models. He writes both numbers with clear labels, then explains why adding observations is not always the same as counting different objects.

For the museum game, Rafi must cite clues supporting a location. He rejects the storage room even though it is dry and has a clock, because it fails the visitor-access requirement. Meeting two of three requirements is not enough. At the end, he checks each answer against every relevant condition and underlines any step that depends on information the passage never supplied.

Day 209 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

A Window in the Last Line

以敘事上下文理解象徵語句與人物情緒轉折。

The class reads a short story about a student moving to a new town. For most of the story, the student describes rooms, streets, and faces as unfamiliar. In the final scene, a neighbor invites the student to help plant flowers. The last line says, 'For the first time, the town had a window.'

Kai draws a literal window beside his answer and writes that a building was repaired. His partner asks where the text mentions construction. They reread the invitation and notice that the student has just found a possible connection with someone.

Kai changes his explanation. The window may suggest a new opening toward belonging rather than a change to a wall. His teacher asks him to support that reading with the invitation and earlier loneliness. Another interpretation is possible, she says, but it still needs to fit the surrounding details. An imaginative answer is strongest when it remains connected to the text.

Day 210 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Space Left Empty in the Suitcase

推論物品安排反映的經驗與人物決策。

Before a family trip, Poppy fills every corner of her suitcase. She packs three books, extra shoes, and several things she says she might possibly need. Her father asks where she will put the small gifts she plans to bring home.

Poppy remembers their last trip, when she carried a torn paper bag because nothing more would fit. She removes one book she has already read and a pair of shoes nearly identical to another pair. A small empty space appears beside her clothes.

During the trip, she uses that space for a handmade bowl wrapped carefully in soft fabric. The empty space was not a forgotten item or wasted effort; it was part of her plan. Poppy does not decide to pack almost nothing next time. She learns that preparation includes considering what may happen later, and that leaving room can be a deliberate choice rather than a failure to fill a container.

Day 211 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

The Date with a Question Mark

辨識暫定資訊與確定安排，推論標記的功能。

[Band chat] Elise: The rehearsal calendar says 'Thursday 4:00?' Is that confirmed? Tao: I copied it into my phone without the question mark. I assumed the mark was just a typing mistake. Elise: The room request is still being checked.

Tao: Then I shouldn't tell everyone it is final. Elise: Right. The coordinator will confirm both the room and time tomorrow. Until then, keep it as a possible slot. We also need to ask whether the drummer can attend.

Tao changes his calendar entry to 'provisional' and posts a correction where he shared the earlier message. When confirmation arrives, he will replace the tentative entry rather than create a second event. The small question mark carried important meaning. Removing it made the message look cleaner, but it also removed the uncertainty that other members needed when planning their afternoon.

Day 212 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Blank Hours on the Weather Sheet

區分未記錄與數值零，判斷缺失資料的影響。

A class keeps a daily sheet of rainfall readings from a model weather station. Monday shows four units, Tuesday shows zero, and Wednesday is blank. The note below Wednesday says the recorder was switched off during the observation period.

Faye enters zero for Wednesday while preparing a chart. Her partner asks whether a blank caused by missing observation means no rain. Faye checks the note and realizes that Tuesday and Wednesday represent different situations: one was measured, while the other was not.

They leave Wednesday marked 'no data' and explain the gap below the chart. They can total the recorded Monday and Tuesday amounts, but cannot claim that this is the complete total for all three days. The class learns that an empty space can contain important information about how much is known. Replacing it with a convenient number would create a result the observations never supplied.

Day 214 · 每週 Boss · 15 分鐘

Boss: Seventy Selections from Fifty Students

統整多選調查數據、填答人數與可支持的結論。

[Form rules] Each respondent selected either one or two different workshop topics. Choices were not ranked. Each student submitted exactly one valid form. The center surveyed fifty students and received a response from every one of them.

[Results] Art received thirty selections, Science received twenty-five, and Games received fifteen. These seventy selections came from the fifty respondents. The form did not ask why they chose a topic or which selected topic they liked best.

[Planning note] Art has the largest count, but a session still depends on finding a teacher and room. The center will contact possible teachers before announcing any booking. Interest is evidence for planning, not a promise that a workshop will run.

The team checks both counts and wording before writing its report. It can compare selections and calculate how many people chose two topics, but it cannot invent ranked preferences or reasons absent from the form.

Day 215 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Missing Mark and the Missing Number

複習暫定、空白與未排序資料，避免自行補足未知。

Emi's review has five key words: provisional, blank, respondents, ranked, and absent. She sorts mistakes into two types: removing information that was present and adding information that was never provided. Some mistakes, she discovers, do both.

Deleting a question mark from a provisional rehearsal time removes uncertainty. Turning a blank weather entry into zero adds an unsupported measurement. Emi keeps the date tentative and labels the unmeasured day clearly so later readers can distinguish what is known.

The workshop survey has fifty respondents and seventy selections. Emi does not mistake selections for people or assume choices were ranked. Reasons for the choices are absent, so she leaves them unexplained rather than inventing a story. Her final check asks whether a summary preserves the original meaning, including limits. A shorter report can be useful, but only if shortening it has not made its claims stronger than the evidence.

Day 216 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

Disagreeing with a Friend's Proposal

從對話與行動區分意見批評及人際否定。

During a class meeting, Huan questions his friend Lea's plan to spend the whole activity budget on one large concert. He asks what would remain for students who prefer smaller workshops. Lea becomes quiet and avoids him after the meeting.

Huan later says he likes the idea of a concert but is uncertain about using every available dollar. He suggests keeping part of the budget for other activities. Lea admits she had heard his question as a rejection of her effort, not as a concern about the plan.

They review the proposal together and prepare two versions with different spending patterns. The class can now compare trade-offs instead of choosing between total approval and total rejection. Lea still hopes for a concert, and Huan still wants room for workshops. Their friendship does not require identical opinions; it becomes easier when they explain what they are questioning and why.

Day 217 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

Do You Want Advice or a Listener?

理解談話目的與回應方式如何配合對方需求。

After a disappointing school day, Ellis tells his older cousin about a group project that went badly. His cousin immediately offers five ways to reorganize the team. Ellis stops talking and says, 'I know there are things to try. I just wanted you to understand why I'm upset.'

The cousin puts down her notebook and asks whether Ellis wants advice now or someone to listen first. He chooses listening. She asks what part felt hardest and repeats his concern to check that she has understood it.

After a while, Ellis asks for help planning a conversation with his teammates. This time, they discuss one next step together. The cousin's earlier suggestions were not necessarily useless; their timing did not match his immediate purpose. She learns to ask what kind of support is wanted, and Ellis learns that stating his need can help another person respond more usefully.

Day 218 · 對話／訊息 · 10 分鐘

The Run That Needed No Running

利用對話及任務描述推測片語的非字面意思。

[Event chat] Luca: Please arrive at three for a dry run of the welcome ceremony. Wen: Should I bring running shoes? Is it outdoors? Luca: Sorry, 'dry run' means a practice of the procedure. We will walk through the introductions and check the microphones in the hall.

Wen: So guests are not attending yet? Luca: Right. We will use classmates as pretend guests. If a step is confusing, we can stop and adjust it. The real ceremony starts at five, after we have made any needed changes.

Wen adds a plain-language explanation beneath the original reminder. Another new volunteer thanks her because he had been unsure too. Luca realizes that a phrase familiar to experienced organizers may be unclear to others. The practice is useful before anyone enters the hall: it reveals a communication problem while there is still time to fix it.

Day 219 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Shorter Plant That Grew More

區分期末數值與變化量，連同起點比較成長。

In a fictional classroom record, Plant A begins a week at two centimeters and ends at eight. Plant B begins at six and ends at ten. Both are measured from the soil line to the highest point using the same method over the same seven days.

A student says Plant B grew more because it is taller at the end. Her partner calculates the changes: A gained six centimeters, while B gained four. The final height and the amount of growth answer different questions.

The class labels two columns, 'final height' and 'change in height,' instead of placing every number under 'best plant.' They also avoid claiming that one plant type always grows faster from this pair alone. The record can describe these two plants during this week. Keeping the starting values makes that description more informative and prevents a larger final number from hiding a smaller change.

The Seed Library Is an Invitation

COMMUNITY SEED LIBRARY: Take one free packet to try growing something at home. You do not need to return the same number of seeds later. Sharing seeds from a successful harvest is welcome, but it is an invitation rather than a debt.

Each packet lists its suggested light conditions, container space, and expected range of growth. Read the label before choosing. The photographs show examples, not a promise that every plant will look identical. Ask a helper if you are unsure how a label fits your available space.

Please write the packet name in the borrowing notebook so the center can track which supplies need replacing. This record does not reserve more packets for you. If your first attempt fails, you may describe what happened to the helper. The library encourages learning and honest records, not pretending that every seed grew successfully.

Day 222 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

Minimum Does Not Mean Maximum

複習演練、成長量及最低門檻，精準判讀限制詞。

Five words appear in Nao's review: procedure, growth, debt, minimum, and measured. She first explains that a dry run practices a procedure rather than testing running speed. A phrase can be misleading when its words are read without their setting.

For the plant record, Nao separates final height from growth. A plant moving from two to eight centimeters grew six, even if another ended taller. She also remembers that the seed library invites sharing without creating a debt to return equal seeds.

The final task compares a measured four hours of light with a minimum requirement of four. Nao says the light condition is met, then checks container width separately. Equality satisfies 'at least,' but one suitable condition does not prove every requirement is met. Her review ends with a habit of circling limit words before choosing an option, especially when several numbers look close.

Day 223 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Promise in Last Year's Envelope

比較前後書面紀錄，推論學習進展與目標修訂。

At the end of term, the teacher returns envelopes students sealed a year earlier. Inside, each student wrote one hope and one worry. June's note says she hopes to speak perfectly in front of the class and worries that one mistake will make everyone laugh.

June has given three short presentations since then. She made mistakes in all of them, but she also answered questions and learned to continue after losing a word. Her old goal now seems both understandable and impossible to measure fairly.

She writes a new note: 'I want to explain one idea clearly, check whether listeners understand, and recover when I get stuck.' This promise does not sound as grand as perfection. It gives her actions she can practice and evidence she can look for. June keeps both notes because the difference between them shows something her presentation scores alone would not reveal: how her understanding of improvement has changed.

Day 224 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Queue with Two Different Signs

整合取件與諮詢流程，推論不同等候順序的原因。

At a community repair desk, Max takes a number and waits with his broken lamp. A woman who arrives later walks to another counter and leaves almost immediately with a repaired radio. Max feels that she has unfairly gone ahead of him.

Before complaining, he reads the two signs. His counter says 'New repair requests: take a number.' The other says 'Collection of completed items: show your receipt.' The woman was collecting work arranged on an earlier visit, not joining the queue for a new assessment.

Max asks the helper to confirm which line he needs and keeps his number. He still hopes the wait will be short, but he no longer treats the woman's quick departure as evidence of unfairness. The room contains two services with different steps. Seeing who arrived first was not enough to understand which order applied to each person.

Day 226 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

A Larger Picture Is Not More Detail

辨識影像放大與新增證據的差異。

In a media lesson, students inspect a small photograph of a distant sign. The letters are unclear. Owen enlarges the image on the screen and says the bigger version should reveal every word, but the letters become larger blocks rather than clearer shapes.

The teacher explains that this copy contains only the information already recorded in its limited detail. Enlarging the display does not by itself recover letters that cannot be distinguished. A student suggests returning to the original higher-quality photograph or asking the photographer for a closer view.

The class marks the uncertain text as unreadable instead of inventing a likely slogan. They can describe the visible color and position of the sign, but cannot quote its full message confidently. The lesson is about matching claims to the information available. A larger presentation can make existing evidence easier to inspect without necessarily adding new evidence.

Kira's review words are genuine, unreadable, direction, fare, and workable. Her cards contain a real old screenshot, an enlarged blurry sign, and a festival bus poster. Each looks useful until she asks what decision its evidence can support.

The genuine screenshot describes August maintenance, so Kira does not use it to decide an October visit. The enlarged sign remains unreadable, so she describes visible features without inventing a quotation. More confidence would not add the missing information.

Day 230 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

The Question after the Final Slide

由簡報後的問答推論理解深度與適當回應。

Ronan finishes a class presentation and feels relieved when the final slide appears. He has memorized every sentence. Then a classmate asks how his recommendation would change if the budget were smaller. Ronan looks back at the slide, but the exact answer is not written there.

His teacher gives him time to think. Ronan identifies the recommendation's purpose and the two costs that mattered most. He says which part he would keep first and which part would need a cheaper alternative. He also names a price he would have to check before deciding.

The answer is less smooth than his prepared speech, but it shows how he connects information. After class, Ronan adds a page of possible questions to his notes. He does not try to memorize every imaginable reply. He practices explaining the reasons behind his choices so he can use them when a new condition appears.

Finished Reading, Finished Answering

比較信心與正確性，從回饋辨識需要重查的判斷。

In a fictional practice lesson, students answer six reading questions and mark each answer 'sure,' 'unsure,' or 'guess.' They check the answers only after finishing. The confidence marks do not change their scores; they provide another way to inspect the result.

Yani gets four questions right. Two were answers she felt sure about, one was unsure, and one was a guess. Of her two wrong answers, one had been marked sure. She is surprised because strong confidence had felt like proof.

The teacher asks Yani to compare her reasons with the passage. She finds that the confidently wrong answer used a familiar word but reversed a condition. She also explains why the guessed answer happened to be correct. The exercise does not label confidence as useless. It helps Yani notice when confidence needs checking and when a correct letter still hides incomplete understanding.

Day 236 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

Why the First Answer Still Matters

複習完成狀態、信心與修改證據，規劃後續練習。

At review, Dia writes five words beside her practice sheet: completion, confidence, reasoning, revision, and textual. She used to erase every wrong first answer until only a clean page remained. Now she keeps a small mark showing where her thinking changed.

A correct revision with textual evidence tells her more than a changed letter alone. She compares the first reasoning with the later reasoning and asks whether she misunderstood a condition, ignored a heading, or guessed from a repeated word. Confidence is another clue to inspect, not a substitute for checking.

Dia also defines completion carefully. Finishing a passage, answering questions, and explaining evidence are different steps. She chooses one recurring mistake for her next short practice instead of treating the whole subject as a single weakness. Her page looks less perfect, but it gives a clearer picture of what she can work on next.

Day 237 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

Two Scores from Different Papers

比較分數時考慮題數、難度與技能構成。

Ria scores eighteen out of twenty on one practice paper and thirty out of forty on another. She points to thirty and says her performance clearly improved because the number of correct answers is larger. Her friend asks how many questions each paper contained.

They calculate ninety percent for the first and seventy-five percent for the second. Ria then says she must have become worse. The teacher asks them to look at the questions too. The second paper contains longer passages and more inference tasks, so the percentages alone do not describe a controlled comparison.

Ria checks which skills she missed on each paper and plans a similar set for a later comparison. She keeps the scores with their denominators and task descriptions. A number becomes more useful when its context travels with it. Neither a larger raw count nor a smaller percentage can by itself explain every change in her reading.

Day 238 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Small Task That Finally Started

從行動順序推論目標拆分如何影響人物行為。

Sam keeps writing 'Improve my English' at the top of his weekend list. The phrase feels important, but when Saturday arrives he cannot decide where to begin. He opens several books, changes his mind, and spends more time choosing than reading.

This week, he writes a smaller action: read one short passage and explain why one tempting wrong option is wrong. He puts the passage and a pencil on his desk the night before. The task has a visible starting point and a clear ending.

After finishing, Sam chooses whether to continue. Sometimes he reads another passage; sometimes he stops and returns later. The smaller task does not cover every English skill or guarantee a particular result. It helps him turn a broad wish into an action he can repeat. By Sunday, he has something more useful than a large unchecked promise: a record of several completed, explained attempts.

Day 240 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Hundred Percent Success Poster

連同比例、次數與測試條件判讀百分比宣稱。

In a fictional paper-airplane activity, Team Red reports that its plane reached a target in one of one trial. Team Blue reports eight successes in ten trials. A poster calls Red's design 'the best' because its success rate is one hundred percent, while Blue's is eighty percent.

The teacher asks students to include the numbers behind the percentages. Red has only one recorded attempt, so its perfect percentage gives little information about repeated performance. Blue's ten trials provide more observations, though conditions still need checking before a fair design comparison.

The teams plan additional trials with the same target distance and agreed launch procedure. They will keep unsuccessful attempts in the record as well as successes. The activity does not show that Red's plane is poor. It shows why a striking percentage should be read together with the amount and quality of evidence behind it.

Final Practice Room Choices

整合練習場次、材料版本及進場規定。

FINAL PRACTICE ROOMS: Choose one thirty-minute session on Saturday. Room Cedar starts at 9:00 and 10:00. Room Maple starts at 9:30 and 10:30. Both rooms use the same practice passage and questions, but option order may differ between printed versions.

Arrive at least five minutes before your chosen start. Doors close when the session begins so the room can remain quiet. You may reserve one place only. If you change sessions, release the old place before confirming another.

After the timed session, an optional fifteen-minute discussion takes place in the same room. Check your paper's version before using the answer key. A printed explanation sheet is available afterward for students who cannot stay. The discussion and the sheet cover the same reasoning, so leaving after the session does not prevent you from reviewing the evidence later.

Compare the Meaning, Then the Number

Ivo reviews five words: version, trial, optional, limits, and availability. He starts with two answer sheets showing different letters for the same question. Before deciding who is wrong, he compares the version names, option wording, and supporting sentence.

Next, he sees a one-hundred-percent result based on one trial and an eighty-percent result based on ten. He keeps the counts beside the rates and avoids declaring a permanent winner. The numbers describe the recorded attempts, not every possible future performance.

For a practice-room plan, Ivo includes the optional discussion because the fictional student wants to attend it. He checks arrival and leaving limits as well as seat availability. Day 244 · 校園故事 · 10 分鐘

A Letter to Next Year's Reader

從建議信推論寫作目的、對象與可操作的閱讀方法。

The graduating class leaves advice for next year's reading club. Instead of writing 'Work harder,' Elin writes about a mistake she remembers clearly: choosing an option because it repeated a word from the passage, even though the relationship was wrong.

She tells the next reader to find a sentence that supports the whole answer, not just one familiar word. She also suggests marking uncertain choices and returning to them after reading the surrounding paragraph. Her letter includes a small example and an explanation of why the tempting option fails.

Elin does not promise that this method will solve every question or predict a grade. She says it helped her notice a specific habit and gives the next reader something to try. At the end, she leaves space for a reply from the future club. Advice, she decides, becomes more useful when another person can test it, adapt it, and add what they discover.

Day 245 · 日常生活 · 10 分鐘

The Map Drawn from Your Own Door

從接收者視角檢查指示，辨識依賴共享背景的語句。

Finn draws directions for a friend visiting his neighborhood. He writes, 'Turn right at the usual shop, then walk toward our old meeting place.' To Finn, the route is obvious. His friend has never visited, so neither landmark means anything to her.

She asks for street names and a starting point. Finn redraws the route from the bus stop where she will arrive, labels the bakery's actual name, and describes the blue entrance across from it. He checks the directions by walking them himself.

When his friend arrives, she says the revised map was easy to follow. Finn notices that the distance has not changed, but the explanation now begins with the reader's knowledge instead of his own. He keeps the first draft as a reminder that clear directions are not simply clear in the writer's head; they must connect with what the other person can identify.

The Answer We Changed for a Reason

從同儕討論判斷改答是否依據文本而非人數。

[Final review chat] Noor: Three people chose B, so should we all use it? Eli: Before changing, let's each show a supporting sentence. My answer is D because the notice says the offer ends before the afternoon session.

Noor: I chose B because the afternoon time was the largest number on the poster. I missed the word 'before.' Another reader checks the date heading and confirms they are discussing the same version. Together they reread the complete condition rather than vote on the letters.

Noor changes her answer and records why. Eli also checks whether his explanation covers every part of D, not just the deadline. Their discussion is useful because agreement follows shared evidence. A majority may be right, but the number of people choosing an option cannot replace the work of showing why that option fits the passage.

Day 247 · 科普閱讀 · 10 分鐘

The Result We Could Not Repeat Yet

分辨單次成果、重複觀察與仍待查明的原因。

In a fictional classroom test, a team's paper bridge holds twelve small blocks before bending. On a second attempt with the same design, a new bridge holds nine. The students want to keep only the first result because it makes their project look stronger.

The teacher asks them to record both attempts and compare how the bridges were made. One fold was slightly different, and the blocks may not have been placed in exactly the same positions. These observations suggest questions to check; they do not prove which difference caused the lower result.

The team plans another attempt using a written folding procedure and marked block positions. It will report the range of results and the conditions used. Repeating the activity may help clarify the pattern, but the next result is not known in advance. A trustworthy report includes inconvenient observations as well as the ones its writers hoped to see.

Day 248 · 公告／資訊閱讀 · 10 分鐘

Bring One Reading Discovery

閱讀成果分享公告，區分參與材料、分享內容與成績宣稱。

READING DISCOVERY EXCHANGE: Bring one passage you have practiced and one question that changed your thinking. You do not need to bring your highest score. Choose an example you can explain with words from the passage, including why another option is less suitable.

Partners will take turns for three minutes each. First describe your original choice, then the clue you noticed, and finally the reason for your current answer. You may cover your name and score before sharing the sheet. Participation does not require revealing your complete learning record.

After both turns, write one strategy you want to try on a different passage. The exchange celebrates explained learning, not a ranking of students or an official exam prediction. Keep your own materials afterward. The goal is to leave with a method you can test, rather than a comparison of whose page looks most impressive.

Final Boss: The Reading Fair Report

[Fair notice] Each pair has six minutes, with three minutes per reader. Share one changed answer and explain the textual clue. Names and scores may be covered. The event is for exchanging methods, not ranking students or predicting official exam levels.

[Pair record] Ava first chose a picnic because that word appeared in the passage. She changed to an indoor visit after noticing 'but finally decided.' Leon first accepted a poster's largest time, then checked the direction heading and revised his bus plan.

[Draft report] Twelve volunteers shared examples. Every volunteer explained one revision. Therefore, every student in the school now understands all reading questions and will reach the same exam level. The editor underlines the final sentence and asks for a narrower conclusion.

The revised report says the twelve participants practiced explaining a changed answer with evidence. It does not claim that one successful explanation establishes every reading skill. Ava and Leon leave with strategies to test on unfamiliar passages, where further practice can show what they have learned.

  2. To avoid examining further evidence.
  3. To see whether they can apply the methods beyond the examples already discussed.
  4. To replace every source with their first guesses.

Day 250 · 單字與錯題復活 · 10 分鐘

The Next Page Is Yours

總複習證據、範圍與學習遷移，建立完成課程後的練習方式。

On the last day of a long reading project, Nia opens a passage she has never seen before. She remembers five words from the final week: supporting, trustworthy, discovery, revision, and unfamiliar. They remind her of actions rather than a list to recite.

She checks the title and conditions, answers independently, and finds a supporting sentence for each choice. One option repeats a familiar word but changes the relationship, so she rejects it. Where the evidence is incomplete, she keeps her explanation limited instead of pretending to know more.

Nia compares her reasoning with the answer notes and records one useful revision. Finishing the project has not ended her learning or guaranteed an exam result. It has given her a routine she can carry to the next page: read carefully, ask what supports an answer, learn from a mistake, and try again in a new context. Her final discovery is that progress can continue after the last numbered day.

1 · 細節理解 · 基礎

What kind of passage does Nia open?

  1. A complete official score report.
  2. A list containing no sentences.
  3. One she has not seen before.
  4. Only the first passage she memorized.

2 · 推論判讀 · 基礎

Why does she reject an option containing a familiar word?

  1. It changes the relationship stated in the passage.
  2. Familiar words are always wrong.
  3. The option has no letters.
  4. The title forbids vocabulary questions.

3 · 細節理解 · 基礎

What does she record after comparing explanations?

  1. A guaranteed exam level.
  2. A promise never to read again.
  3. Every classmate's private score.
  4. One useful revision.

4 · 字義推測 · 基礎

What does 'unfamiliar' mean?

  1. Already memorized exactly.
  2. Impossible for anyone to understand.
  3. Not previously known or recognized.
  4. Written without a title.

5 · 推論判讀 · 進階

What does Nia do when evidence is incomplete?

  1. Treat every blank as zero.
  2. Limit the explanation to what is supported.
  3. Invent details to make a confident answer.
  4. Assume the first guess is certain.

6 · 主旨統整 · 挑戰

What is the final lesson of the project?

  1. Completion guarantees a particular official result.
  2. No further reading is needed after the last lesson.
  3. Remembering five words replaces checking evidence.
  4. A practiced reading routine can support continued learning beyond Day 250.
